Wilton, Senn, Sharma, and Tan (2015) conducted a comprehensive review of the use of PrEP for managing sexually acquired HIV risk. Their work, published in HIV AIDS (Auckland), provided an in-depth analysis of the effectiveness and implementation of PrEP strategies. Young and McDaid (2014) reviewed research on the acceptability of oral PrEP and treatment-as-prevention approaches. UNAIDS held a consultation meeting in Johannesburg in November 2013 to explore the hopes and concerns of sex workers regarding PrEP for HIV prevention. Recommendations from this meeting were developed in collaboration with the Wits Reproductive Health and HIV Institute. The International Network of People Who Use Drugs (2014) published a report discussing harm reduction, hepatitis C, and PrEP from the perspective of the drug-using community. This document emphasized the unique challenges and opportunities for implementing PrEP in this population. Nwagwu, Georges, and Weathers (2013) investigated perceived barriers to adopting PrEP among male-to-female transgender youth. Their findings were presented in the Communicating Nursing Research journal. Van der Straten, Stadler, Montgomery, and colleagues (2014) conducted the VOICE-C qualitative study in Johannesburg, South Africa, to explore women’s experiences with oral and vaginal PrEP. Their research, published in PLOS One, provided valuable insights into the acceptability and challenges of these interventions. Bekker, Hughes, Amico, Grant, and others presented findings from the HPTN 067/ADAPT Cape Town study at the 2015 Conference on Retroviruses and Opportunistic Infections in Seattle. This study compared daily and non-daily PrEP dosing among African women. UNITAID published the second edition of its report on the HIV prevention technology and market landscape in November 2014. This document provided an overview of the global market and technological advancements in HIV prevention. Gomez, Borquez, Case, Wheelock, Vassall, and colleagues (2013) conducted a systematic review of cost-effectiveness modeling studies on scaling up PrEP for HIV prevention. Their findings, published in PLOS Medicine, assessed the financial and public health impacts of widespread PrEP implementation. Alistar, Owens, and Brandeau (2014) evaluated the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of oral PrEP as part of a portfolio of prevention programs for injection drug users in mixed HIV epidemics. Their study, published in PLOS One, provided evidence to guide resource allocation in HIV prevention. Grant, Lama, Goicochea, Levy, Marseille, and others presented a cost-effectiveness analysis of HIV chemoprophylaxis at the 2006 World AIDS Conference in Toronto. Their findings emphasized the economic feasibility of oral PrEP in preventing HIV transmission. The World Health Organization (WHO) has been developing antiretroviral therapy (ART) guidelines since 2002, carefully considering the available evidence to address the limited availability of antiretroviral drugs in many countries. The current systematic review updates previous reviews and evaluates the clinical impact of initiating ART earlier in HIV-1-infected patients with a higher CD4 threshold (≥500 cells/μL). The systematic review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and cohort studies comparing clinical and laboratory outcomes in patients initiating ART at different CD4 thresholds. The outcomes assessed included mortality, severe HIV disease, malignancy, clinical progression, AIDS events, non-AIDS events, tuberculosis, severe treatment-related adverse events, and HIV transmission. The review identified 20 studies, including three reports from a single RCT. The quality of evidence was moderate for combined outcomes such as mortality and severe HIV disease or malignancy, but low or very low for other clinical and adverse event outcomes due to indirectness and imprecision. The findings suggest that earlier ART initiation is associated with a lower risk of HIV disease progression and transmission to uninfected partners. However, the evidence quality for these outcomes varies, with moderate evidence supporting the lack of increased risk for severe adverse events and very low evidence indicating potential liver-related adverse events. The review highlights the need for further research, including ongoing RCTs such as the START trial, to provide more definitive evidence on the optimal timing of ART initiation. These findings will inform the 2015 WHO guidelines on antiretroviral drug use for HIV treatment and prevention.
